opus-5.5.text:
I think the shift in naming really reflects a shift in where we believe the core problem lies.

When people say "robotics," the traditional emphasis has been on the body itself: the mechanical design, the actuators, the control theory, how you make a joint move precisely along a trajectory. For decades, a lot of the field's progress was about building better hardware and better controllers for well-defined tasks. Think of an industrial arm on an assembly line. It's extremely precise, extremely reliable, but it has essentially no intelligence. It repeats what it's been programmed to do in a highly structured environment.

"Embodied intelligence" puts the emphasis on the intelligence, but intelligence that is grounded in a physical body interacting with the real world. The key idea is that intelligence doesn't just live in a disembodied model that reads text or looks at images. A truly general intelligence needs to perceive the world, act in it, get feedback from those actions, and learn from that loop. The body isn't just a vehicle for executing commands. It's part of how intelligence is formed and expressed.

There's also a historical context here. With large language models, we've seen what happens when you scale up learning on internet data: you get remarkable generalization in the digital world. The natural question is, can we bring that kind of generality into the physical world? Can a robot walk into a home it has never seen, face objects it has never touched, and still figure out what to do? That's fundamentally an intelligence problem, not just a mechanical one. So calling it embodied intelligence signals that we're trying to build a general-purpose brain for physical agents, not just a better machine.

And I'd say the hardest part is exactly there. In the digital world you have enormous amounts of data. In the physical world, data is scarce, expensive to collect, and every interaction takes real time. So a big part of our work, for example using simulation and synthetic data at scale, is about solving the data problem so that this intelligence can actually emerge. The name, in a way, tells you where the bottleneck is and where the excitement is: it's in the brain, and in how that brain learns through a body.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the shift in naming is really telling about where the emphasis has moved. When we said "robotics," the center of gravity was the body, the hardware. It was a mechanical engineering and control discipline. You designed a machine, you modeled its dynamics precisely, and you wrote controllers to make it track a trajectory. Intelligence, if it was there at all, was a layer added on top, and usually a very thin one, hand-coded for a specific task in a specific environment.

"Embodied intelligence" flips that. The subject is intelligence, and "embodied" is the modifier. The claim is that intelligence is the core thing we're building, and the body is the means by which that intelligence meets the physical world. So it's really a statement that this field now belongs, at least in large part, to the AI community, and that the questions driving it are AI questions: how does an agent perceive, how does it learn, how does it generalize to situations it has never seen.

There's a second, deeper point in the word "embodied." For a long time, AI was disembodied. Language models, vision models, they live on the internet, on text and images that humans produced. An embodied agent has to close the loop. It acts, the world responds, and it has to deal with the consequences in real time, with noise, with contact, with gravity. Many of us believe that this closed loop with the physical world is actually essential to intelligence itself, that a lot of what we call common sense comes from having a body and interacting through it. In that sense "embodied intelligence" isn't just a rebranding of robots. It's saying this may be a necessary path toward more general intelligence.

And practically, the name reflects a change in method. In classical robotics, if the robot failed, you went back and tuned the model or the controller. In embodied intelligence, the answer is almost always more data, better learning, better representations. The robot is becoming a platform for a learned policy, more like how a GPU is a platform for a neural network. That doesn't mean hardware stops mattering. It matters enormously. But the bottleneck has moved from "can the machine physically do it" to "does the machine understand what it should do."

astra-6.text:
I think the emphasis is on intelligence. When we say “robotics,” people often think first of the machine: its motors, mechanisms, sensors, and control systems. “Embodied intelligence” brings a different question to the foreground: how can an agent perceive, learn, and act through a physical body while interacting with the world?

For example, picking up a cup is not just recognizing where the cup is and executing a fixed motion. You need to judge how to grasp it, respond when it slips, and adjust if it is heavier than expected. Perception and action form a continuous loop. Your actions change what you perceive, and that feedback changes your next action.

Of course, robotics has always studied these problems too, so I wouldn’t draw a sharp boundary. The change in terminology signals an ambition: moving from machines engineered to perform specific tasks toward agents that can adapt to unfamiliar objects, tasks, and environments. The body is not merely a platform carrying an AI model; interacting through that body is part of how the intelligence works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the emphasis shifts from the machine itself to the intelligence that emerges through interaction with the physical world. When we say robotics, people often picture a particular piece of hardware: a robot arm, a quadruped, or a humanoid. Embodied intelligence puts the focus on how an agent perceives, acts, and learns through its body.

The key is that perception and action form a loop. You don’t just look at an object and produce an answer; you reach for it, discover that it’s heavier or more slippery than expected, and adjust. Your actions also help you gather information.

So I see the terms as overlapping, rather than competing. Robotics already studies these questions. But calling it embodied intelligence highlights the ambition to build systems whose understanding is grounded in interaction, and whose abilities can generalize beyond a single carefully defined task.
